name: Cycloastragenol

angle.text: Cycloastragenol is marketed as a telomerase activator for slowing ageing, which users hope shows up as a younger look. Support comes from cell and animal work. No trials have tested its effect on appearance.

summary: A purified astragalus saponin marketed as a telomerase activator; mostly cell and animal data, no appearance trials.
note: Human safety not well established; the FTC has acted against ageing-reversal advertising for TA-65.
currentQuick:
Cycloastragenol is the sugar-free form of astragaloside IV, a compound from astragalus root. It is sold as a longevity supplement because of claims that it activates telomerase.
The evidence is mainly preclinical. A small human study exists on a related telomerase-activator product, but no trial tests it for appearance or skin ageing.
How it works: It is reported to raise telomerase (TERT) activity in cells through MAPK/ERK and related signalling, and to dampen inflammasome-driven inflammation in animal models.
Risks and caveats: Toxicity data are limited and human safety has not been adequately shown. A theoretical concern exists because telomerase is active in most cancers. The FTC issued a consent order over ageing-reversal advertising for the branded product TA-65.
deepLead:
Cycloastragenol is a tetracyclic triterpenoid obtained from the roots of Astragalus species, notably Astragalus membranaceus. It is the aglycone (sugar-free form) of astragaloside IV, a major saponin of the herb used in traditional Chinese medicine. It is marketed as a supplement ingredient on the claim that it activates telomerase, the enzyme that extends the protective ends of chromosomes.
Wikipedia describes the telomerase-activation claim as not well established: a preliminary study on human T cells reported a moderate increase in telomerase activity, and the clinical significance is uncertain. Most research on the compound is preclinical, covering inflammation, neuroprotection, cardiovascular and cancer models in cells and rodents.
No study found in these sources tests cycloastragenol for facial appearance, skin or hair outcomes in people.

name: Astragalus

chain: Tonic herb for immunity and vitality
angle.text: Astragalus root (huangqi) is a classic Chinese tonic taken as an immune and anti-ageing herb, and longevity enthusiasts include it in stacks aimed at ageing well. Its use is traditional and general; no appearance trials exist.

summary: The root behind huangqi, a classic Chinese tonic herb; promoted for longevity and immunity, with no appearance trials.
note: Evidence is largely preclinical; other Astragalus species are toxic to livestock.
currentQuick:
Astragalus root (huangqi) is a staple tonic herb in traditional Chinese medicine, now sold as a longevity and immune-support supplement.
Reviews describe immune, antioxidant and metabolic effects, mostly from lab and animal work. Human trials are few and small, and none tests appearance outcomes.
How it works: Its polysaccharides, astragalosides and isoflavones are reported to modulate immune signalling and inflammation in cell and animal models. Astragaloside IV is metabolised to cycloastragenol, sold separately as a telomerase activator.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia states the toxic constituents of other Astragalus species were not found in the species used in supplements. Human adverse-effect data are not well covered in the sources reviewed; product quality and adulteration are noted in chemical analyses.
deepLead:
Astragalus, in this entry, refers to the root of Astragalus membranaceus (also Astragalus mongholicus or A. propinquus), known in traditional Chinese medicine as huangqi. It is a perennial legume native to temperate Asia, and the root is one of the best-known tonic herbs in Chinese and Mongolian traditional medicine. It is promoted in the longevity-supplement category as an immune and anti-ageing tonic.
Its main constituents are polysaccharides, saponins such as astragaloside IV, and isoflavones including calycosin and formononetin. Reviews describe immune-stimulant, antioxidant, antidiabetic and other activities, mostly from laboratory and animal work.
Wikipedia reports limited clinical evidence for Astragalus products. No study found in these sources tests astragalus for facial appearance, skin or hair outcomes.

name: Gynostemma pentaphyllum (jiaogulan)

angle.text: Jiaogulan tea and extracts are used as a ginseng-like adaptogen in longevity routines. Users link general health and stress resilience with ageing well. Evidence is mostly lab-based with thin human data and no appearance trials.

summary: A sweet adaptogen tea vine with ginseng-like saponins; lab-rich, human data thin, no appearance trials.
note: Human toxicity data are lacking; EU treats it as a novel food.
currentQuick:
Jiaogulan is a climbing vine whose leaves are brewed as a sweet tea and sold as an adaptogen and longevity herb. It contains gypenosides, some chemically identical to ginseng saponins.
Research is mostly in cells and animals, with small preliminary human trials on blood sugar and weight. None tests appearance.
How it works: Gypenosides and polysaccharides are reported to have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in laboratory models, including damping of NLRP3 inflammasome signalling.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia states there is no information on human toxicity, with toxicity data only in vitro. In the EU it is regulated as a novel food.
deepLead:
Gynostemma pentaphyllum, called jiaogulan or "five-leaf ginseng", is a climbing vine in the gourd family (Cucurbitaceae) native to South and East Asia and New Guinea. It is usually drunk as a sweet herbal tea and also sold as extracts and supplements, and is grouped with adaptogen herbs in the longevity category.
Its leaves contain dammarane-type saponins, some identical to ginseng ginsenosides and others called gypenosides, plus polysaccharides, flavonoids and sterols. Laboratory studies report antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, liver-protective and cardiometabolic effects.
Wikipedia states that research is limited, that studies in cardiovascular disease, hyperlipidaemia and type 2 diabetes were too preliminary to conclude benefit, and that no information exists on human toxicity. No study found in these sources tests jiaogulan for appearance outcomes.

name: Schisandra chinensis

angle.text: Schisandra berry extract is taken as an adaptogen in longevity circles, valued for antioxidant and liver-support properties. The link to looks is general healthy ageing. Studies are mainly lab-based on the liver and antioxidants, with nothing on appearance.

summary: The five-flavour berry of Chinese and Russian tonic tradition; liver and antioxidant lab data, nothing on looks.
note: Human trials are few and mostly in combination formulas.
currentQuick:
Schisandra is a vine whose berries are used as a tonic in Chinese, Korean and Russian traditions and sold as an adaptogen supplement.
Laboratory studies report liver-protective, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects. Human trials are small, often of multi-herb formulas, and none addresses appearance.
How it works: Its lignans, such as schisandrin and schisandrin B, are reported in animal and cell studies to act on inflammatory and metabolic signalling, including AMPK/mTOR pathways.
Risks and caveats: Safety and interaction data are not well covered in the sources reviewed. Product identity can vary because S. chinensis and S. sphenanthera are different species.
deepLead:
Schisandra chinensis, the Chinese magnolia vine or five-flavour berry (wuweizi in Chinese, omija in Korean), is a deciduous woody vine native to forests of northern China, the Russian Far East, Korea and Japan. Its red berries are used in traditional medicine and in a Korean cordial drink, and the extract is sold as an adaptogen in the longevity-supplement category.
The berries contain lignans such as schisandrin, deoxyschizandrin and gomisins. A 2008 review summarises Russian research on the plant as a tonic and stimulant, and laboratory studies report liver-protective, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects.
Human evidence is sparse. No study found in these sources tests schisandra for facial appearance, skin or hair outcomes.

name: Rhodiola rosea

angle.text: Rhodiola is taken as an adaptogen for stress and fatigue, so users can stay energised and recover, and some posters discuss effects on testosterone and estrogen. Human trials on fatigue are of mixed quality; its appearance use is untested.

summary: The Arctic adaptogen root sold for stress and fatigue; mixed-quality trials and nothing on appearance.
note: FDA warning letters issued over unapproved health claims; wild populations are overharvested.
currentQuick:
Rhodiola rosea is an Arctic and mountain succulent whose root is sold as an adaptogen for stress, fatigue and stamina. Forum mentions focus on productivity and worries about hormones.
A 2010 review summarised its clinical efficacy, but Wikipedia cites an EMA report describing the published trials as having considerable quality deficiencies. No trial tests appearance outcomes.
How it works: Its rosavins and salidroside are reported in cell and animal studies to have antioxidant, neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory activity, including via Sirt1 signalling.
Risks and caveats: FDA has issued warning letters over unapproved claims. The plant is listed under CITES Appendix II and products can be adulterated. Wikipedia does not discuss human adverse effects, and no study cited here examines hormone effects.
deepLead:
Rhodiola rosea, known as golden root, rose root or Arctic root, is a perennial succulent in the stonecrop family (Crassulaceae) that grows in cold, high-altitude and Arctic regions of Europe, Asia and North America. Its rhizome is used in traditional medicine and sold as an adaptogen: a supplement promoted for stress, fatigue and stamina.
The rhizome contains roughly 140 compounds, including the phenylpropanoids rosavin, rosarin and rosin and the phenylethanoid salidroside. A 2010 review summarised its traditional use, chemistry and clinical efficacy, and laboratory work on salidroside reports neuroprotective, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in cells and animals.
Wikipedia states that researchers have found no high-quality clinical evidence that the plant treats any disease, and cites a 2012 European Medicines Agency report that described published trials as having considerable quality deficiencies. No study found in these sources tests rhodiola for appearance outcomes.

name: Eleutherococcus (Siberian ginseng)

angle.text: Eleuthero is used as an adaptogen for stress and fatigue, with some users believing a calmer stress response shows in their skin and general look. Human evidence on stress is thin, and the appearance link is based on anecdote.

summary: A thorny Asian shrub root sold as a stress-and-fatigue adaptogen; human evidence is thin and nothing ties it to appearance directly.
note: Not a true ginseng; product content varies between brands.
currentQuick:
Eleuthero (Siberian ginseng) is the root of a thorny shrub from East Asia, used in Russian and Chinese herbal traditions as a tonic and sold today as an adaptogen for stress and fatigue.
It is not a true ginseng, and published reviews describe the human evidence as limited and mixed. No trial has tested it for skin or looks.
How it works: Extracts contain eleutherosides, lignans and coumarins. Lab and animal studies report antioxidant and anti-fatigue effects, but the mechanism in people has not been established.
Risks and caveats: Reference summaries list cautions for people with high blood pressure, heart or sleep conditions, and in pregnancy, plus interaction with digoxin. High intake has been linked to irritability and insomnia. Commercial products vary in content. It is sold as a supplement.
deepLead:
Eleutherococcus senticosus, commonly called Siberian ginseng or eleuthero, is a thorny deciduous shrub of the family Araliaceae native to eastern Asia, including China, Japan, Korea and the Russian Far East. Despite the common name it is not a true ginseng: it belongs to a different genus from Panax species such as Asian and American ginseng.
Root extracts are sold as dietary supplements and are classed by supplement marketers as an "adaptogen", a term for substances said to increase resistance to stress. In looksmaxxing-adjacent recovery and wellness discussions it is mentioned as a stress and fatigue aid rather than as a direct appearance treatment.
Published reviews describe the evidence base as limited. The World Health Organization is reported to consider clinical evidence sufficient only for use as a general tonic for weakness, exhaustion and convalescence. Reviews of adaptogens have noted that none of the classic adaptogen plants has been firmly established as a clinical drug. Analyses of commercial ginseng products have found considerable variability in marker-compound content between preparations.

name: Rhaponticum carthamoides (maral root)

angle.text: Maral root is sold to lifters as an ecdysteroid-rich herb to build muscle and speed recovery, and is also used as an adaptogen. Muscle claims rest on animal data and anecdote; no human trial of the herb supports them.

summary: A Siberian herb rich in ecdysteroids that is sold as a muscle and adaptogen supplement; no human trial backs the muscle claims.
note: Not the same as Rheum rhaponticum (rhubarb extract).
currentQuick:
Maral root is a Siberian alpine herb whose roots contain large amounts of 20-hydroxyecdysone, an insect molting hormone. Supplement sellers promote it for strength, recovery and stress resistance.
The published literature is mainly chemistry and lab work; the sources reviewed contain no human trial of it for muscle or appearance.
How it works: The claimed mechanism rests on its ecdysteroid content. Reviews describe antioxidant and other activities in laboratory settings; effects in people have not been established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Safety data in humans are not covered in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a supplement, and products can be confused with Rheum rhaponticum, a different plant.
deepLead:
Rhaponticum carthamoides (synonym Leuzea carthamoides), known as maral root, is a perennial herb of the daisy family (Asteraceae) that grows wild in southern Siberia, Kazakhstan, the Altai and the western Sayan Mountains at sub-alpine and alpine elevations. Its roots are rich in 20-hydroxyecdysone, an ecdysteroid that acts as a molting hormone in arthropods.
It is sold as an adaptogen and, in muscle-building circles, as a source of ecdysteroids. Published literature on the plant is mostly phytochemical and pharmacological reviews, with in vitro and animal work; the sources available for this article identify no completed human trial of maral root for muscle or appearance outcomes.

name: Ganoderma lucidum (Reishi / Lingzhi)

angle.text: Reishi is taken as tea or extract for immunity, stress and sleep, with users hoping better rest improves how they look. Clinical evidence for sleep and immunity is limited, and nothing tests it for appearance directly.

summary: Traditional East Asian medicinal mushroom sold for immunity and sleep; clinical evidence is poor and nothing addresses appearance.
note: Products labelled G. lucidum are often other Ganoderma species.
currentQuick:
Reishi or lingzhi is a woody mushroom used for over two thousand years in East Asian medicine and sold today as tea, extract or capsules for immunity, relaxation and sleep.
A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found no good clinical evidence for cardiovascular or other uses, and no trial has tested it for looks.
How it works: Polysaccharides and triterpenes are thought to be the active constituents, with immune-modulating and antioxidant effects reported in cell and animal studies.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia reports safety concerns and moderate interactions with some medicines and supplements. Product identity varies: DNA testing found many items labelled G. lucidum contained other species. Sold as a supplement.
deepLead:
Ganoderma lucidum, known as reishi in Japan and lingzhi in China, is a bracket fungus used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, in which it was regarded as a mushroom promoting health and longevity. It is taken as tea, extract or capsules and is marketed in wellness and recovery circles as an immune, sleep and stress aid.
Its taxonomy is unsettled: many products and grow kits labelled G. lucidum have been found to contain other species such as G. sichuanense (G. lingzhi). Reviews describe polysaccharides and triterpenes as principal bioactive constituents and report immunomodulatory and anticancer effects mainly in cell and animal work.
A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia concluded that, owing to poor-quality clinical research, there is no good evidence for use of the mushroom in cardiovascular risk or any other medical condition. No trial of reishi for appearance outcomes was identified.

name: Royal jelly

angle.text: Royal jelly is taken as a supplement and used in cosmetics for skin quality and a youthful look. EFSA reviewed the human health claims and found no support, and no trial covers appearance.

summary: Bee-larvae food sold as a skin and wellness supplement; EFSA found no support for human claims and no trial covers appearance.
note: Can cause allergic reactions, rarely anaphylaxis.
currentQuick:
Royal jelly is the secretion nurse bees feed to queen larvae. It is sold as a supplement and cosmetic ingredient and promoted for vitality, skin and general health.
The European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2011 that evidence did not support human health benefits, and no trial of it for appearance was found.
How it works: In bees, royal jelly proteins and diet drive queen development through epigenetic effects. Whether any of this applies to humans is not established; reviews report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in lab settings.
Risks and caveats: Allergic reactions from hives and asthma to fatal anaphylaxis have been reported, with higher risk in allergic people. It is sold as a supplement; the FDA has acted against unsupported health claims.
deepLead:
Royal jelly is a milky secretion produced by the head glands of young worker honey bees (Apis mellifera) and fed to all larvae in their first days and, throughout life, to queen larvae and adult queens. It is harvested commercially and sold as a dietary supplement and a cosmetic ingredient, and is used in apitherapy.
Its composition is roughly two-thirds water, with protein (largely major royal jelly proteins), sugars and lipids including 10-hydroxy-2-decenoic acid (10-HDA), plus B vitamins such as pantothenic acid. Proponents credit it with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and rejuvenating properties, while the European Food Safety Authority concluded in 2011 that evidence did not support health benefits in humans.
Allergic reactions ranging from hives to asthma and, rarely, fatal anaphylaxis have been reported. No human trial of royal jelly for skin or other appearance outcomes was identified in the sources reviewed.

name: Maritime pine bark extract (Pycnogenol)

chain: Less oxidative skin damage, melasma support
angle.text: Pycnogenol is taken as an antioxidant for skin elasticity, hydration and melasma. The link to skin biology is plausible from lab work. Cochrane found insufficient evidence for other uses, and no skin trial was identified.

summary: Pine-bark polyphenol antioxidant floated for skin and melasma; Cochrane found insufficient evidence for other uses and no skin trial turned up.
note: Skin and melasma claims rest on lab antioxidant data.
currentQuick:
Pycnogenol is a branded extract of French maritime pine bark rich in procyanidins, sold as an antioxidant supplement and mentioned for skin and melasma.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for efficacy across the conditions it examined, and the sources reviewed hold no skin or melasma trial.
How it works: Lab studies report free-radical scavenging and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases by its metabolites, the basis for skin-ageing interest. Human skin effects have not been shown in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Safety is not covered in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a dietary supplement, not a drug.
deepLead:
Pycnogenol is the trademarked name of a standardised extract of French maritime pine (Pinus pinaster) bark, composed mainly of proanthocyanidins (procyanidins, about 70%). The term was coined in 1979 by chemist Jack Masquelier, who had extracted proanthocyanidins from pine bark.
It is sold as an antioxidant supplement and is discussed in skin-care circles, including for pigmentation concerns such as melasma. Laboratory work reports free-radical scavenging and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases by its metabolites.
A Cochrane review, updated in 2020 and summarised on Wikipedia, examined uses including asthma, ADHD, blood pressure, osteoarthritis and cognition after brain injury, and found insufficient evidence of efficacy; meta-analyses have likewise found insufficient evidence for any disease. The sources reviewed contain no skin or melasma trial.

name: Grape seed extract

angle.text: Grape seed extract is taken as a polyphenol antioxidant for skin and ageing, and some forum posters use it as a claimed aromatase inhibitor to lower estrogen. The appearance case rests on lab data; no trials test skin or looks.

summary: A grape-derived procyanidin antioxidant; the appearance case rests on lab data, with no trials on skin or looks.
note: Forum aromatase claim comes from cell and mouse studies only.
currentQuick:
Grape seed extract is a supplement made from grape seeds, rich in procyanidin polyphenols. It is sold for antioxidant and vascular support and appears in some skin products.
Human trials are small and look at blood pressure, lipids and exercise rather than appearance. Looksmaxxing forum interest centres on a laboratory finding that it inhibits aromatase.
How it works: Procyanidins scavenge free radicals in laboratory tests and inhibited aromatase and digestive enzymes in cell studies. Absorption of the larger oligomers is limited in animal work.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects are mild (stomach upset, headache) according to secondary sources, with possible interactions with anticoagulants. It is sold as a dietary supplement in the US. Effects on estrogen in humans have not been published.
deepLead:
Grape seed extract (GSE) is a dietary supplement made from the seeds of grapes, mainly Vitis vinifera, which are a by-product of winemaking and grape-juice production. Its polyphenol fraction, typically 5-8% of the seed by weight, consists largely of flavan-3-ols such as catechin and epicatechin and their oligomers and polymers, known as procyanidins or oligomeric proanthocyanidin complexes. 
It is sold as oral capsules and as an ingredient in topical products, and is marketed for antioxidant, vascular and skin-related purposes. In looksmaxxing forums it appears mainly in discussions of skin health and of aromatase inhibition, a claim drawn from laboratory studies. 
Published human trials of GSE are generally small and have examined outcomes such as blood pressure, lipids, vascular stiffness and exercise performance; no published trial found in the sources reviewed tests it for appearance outcomes such as wrinkles or skin tone. Much of the biological work on it comes from cell and animal studies.

name: Genistein

angle.text: Genistein is a soy isoflavone that users consider for skin ageing, since phytoestrogens act on estrogen receptors in skin. It has been studied for many conditions, but trials have not tested it for skin or looks.

summary: A soy phytoestrogen studied for many conditions; no trials test it for skin or looks.
note: Estrogen-receptor activity; cosmetic benefit untested.
currentQuick:
Genistein is the main isoflavone in soy, a plant compound that resembles estrogen. It is sold as a supplement and studied in heart, bone and cancer research.
Its place in appearance discussions is as an antioxidant and phytoestrogen for skin; no trial of cosmetic outcomes has been found.
How it works: It binds estrogen receptors (more strongly to the beta subtype in assays) and inhibits tyrosine kinases in laboratory tests. Oral bioavailability is described as low.
Risks and caveats: Animal studies show estrogen-related effects; human data on hormones are reported as largely reassuring by secondary sources. It is a food component and supplement rather than an approved drug.
deepLead:
Genistein is an isoflavone, a type of plant phytoestrogen, found mainly in soybeans and other legumes. It was first isolated from dyer's broom (Genista tinctoria) in 1899 and has the formula C15H10O5. 
It binds estrogen receptors, with a stronger affinity for estrogen receptor beta than alpha in laboratory binding assays, and it inhibits tyrosine kinase enzymes in vitro.  Dietary interest in it spans cancer prevention, cardiovascular and bone health. 
In appearance and skin contexts it is discussed as a topical or oral antioxidant and phytoestrogen; no published trial located in the sources reviewed tests genistein for wrinkles, skin ageing or other cosmetic outcomes.

name: Diosmin

angle.text: Diosmin is a citrus flavonoid used for leg-vein swelling, and some users try it hoping to reduce fluid retention and puffiness elsewhere, including the face. Its use for venous swelling is studied; face puffiness is untested.

summary: A citrus flavonoid used for leg-vein swelling; interest for face puffiness is untested.
note: Prescription in parts of Europe; no cosmetic trials found.
currentQuick:
Diosmin is a citrus flavonoid used to treat chronic venous insufficiency and haemorrhoids, usually with hesperidin. It is a prescription medicine in parts of Europe and a supplement in the US.
It is listed in bruise and swelling supplements; use for facial puffiness has not been tested.
How it works: It is reported to raise venous tone, reduce capillary permeability and dampen leukocyte-driven inflammation after conversion to diosmetin.
Risks and caveats: Product labels mention mild stomach upset, nausea and rash, rarely bleeding or hypersensitivity. Combination bruise products carry additional warnings for their other ingredients.
deepLead:
Diosmin is a flavonoid glycoside (diosmetin 7-O-rutinoside) found in citrus fruit and first isolated in 1925; it is made commercially by converting hesperidin from citrus peel. 
It is used as a venoactive agent for chronic venous insufficiency, haemorrhoids and leg swelling, often as a micronised purified flavonoid fraction of 90% diosmin and 10% hesperidin; in Europe products such as Daflon are prescription medicines, while in the US it is sold as a supplement. 
In looksmaxxing and appearance contexts it is of interest for swelling, puffiness and bruising. Bruise-support supplements list it alongside arnica, bromelain and vitamin C.  No trial located in the sources reviewed tests diosmin for facial puffiness or other cosmetic outcomes.

name: Krill oil

angle.text: Krill oil is taken as a phospholipid-bound omega-3 source with astaxanthin, for skin and general health. It raises blood EPA and DHA in studies, but effects on skin and looks have not been tested.

summary: A phospholipid-bound omega-3 supplement that raises blood EPA/DHA; its skin and looks effects are untested.
note: Shellfish-derived; fish oil has the larger outcome evidence base.
currentQuick:
Krill oil is an omega-3 supplement from Antarctic krill. Its EPA and DHA are carried on phospholipids, and small trials show it raises blood omega-3 levels comparably to fish oil.
It is discussed for skin and inflammation, but no study has tested it for appearance.
How it works: Phospholipid-bound EPA and DHA are incorporated into plasma phospholipids and the omega-3 index; the claimed advantage over fish oil is better uptake.
Risks and caveats: Fish oil has more outcome trials; krill research is described as newer and smaller. Being crustacean-derived, it is not suited to shellfish-free diets. Harvest is regulated by CCAMLR.
deepLead:
Krill oil is a supplement extracted from Antarctic krill (Euphausia superba), a small crustacean. It supplies the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA largely bound to phospholipids, along with the carotenoid astaxanthin. 
It is compared mostly with fish oil, which carries the omega-3s mainly as triglycerides or ethyl esters. Several small trials report that krill oil raises blood EPA and DHA as effectively as or more than fish oil at lower stated doses, while fish oil has the larger evidence base for outcomes. 
It is listed under skin in the wiki because omega-3 supplements are discussed for skin and inflammation; no published trial located in the sources reviewed tests krill oil for appearance outcomes.

name: Sodium beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB salts)

angle.text: BHB salts are used by people on low-carb diets who hope raised ketones help with appetite and fat loss. They do raise blood BHB; effects on fat loss or looks have not been tested.

summary: Ketone-salt supplements raise blood BHB; fat-loss and looks claims have not been tested.
note: Sodium load; many products are racemic.
currentQuick:
BHB salts are supplements that bind the ketone beta-hydroxybutyrate to minerals such as sodium. They are sold to raise blood ketones without fasting or a ketogenic diet.
Research is limited to small physiology studies, and fat loss from the salts has not been shown in published trials found here.
How it works: BHB is a fuel the body makes during fasting and uses in the brain and muscle. Salts supply it directly, though racemic products contain a form that is less used.
Risks and caveats: Salts add a mineral load (such as sodium) and slightly raise blood pH. Long-term safety data in healthy dieters are limited.
deepLead:
Sodium beta-hydroxybutyrate is a salt form of beta-hydroxybutyrate (BHB), the main ketone body the liver makes during fasting, prolonged exercise and low-carbohydrate diets.  In supplements, BHB is bound to sodium, potassium, magnesium or calcium; most products are racemic, so only about half is the biologically used D form. 
Sellers market ketone salts as a way to raise blood ketones without dietary restriction, with claims about appetite, energy and fat loss.  These claims are commonly discussed in fat-loss contexts.
Human studies of BHB administration are mostly small physiology trials in healthy people and in patients with diabetes or heart failure; none located in the sources reviewed tests BHB salts for fat loss or appearance.

name: Ketone monoester (R-1,3-butanediol ester)

angle.text: The ketone monoester drink is used to raise blood ketones quickly, with fat loss and appetite control as the appearance interest. One study found lower appetite hormones; fat-loss results are unpublished.

summary: The most-studied ketone drink; it lowers appetite hormones in one study, but fat-loss results are unpublished.
note: Fat-loss use untested.
currentQuick:
The ketone monoester is a drink that quickly raises blood beta-hydroxybutyrate. It was developed at the NIH and sold under brands such as KetoneAid.
Human studies cover kinetics, endurance and appetite; fat loss and appearance have not been tested in published trials found here.
How it works: It is broken down into ketone bodies the body can use as fuel, raising blood ketones without fasting or dieting.
Risks and caveats: The 2012 study reported on tolerability in healthy adults. Long-term effects in healthy dieters are not established.
deepLead:
The ketone monoester (R)-3-hydroxybutyl (R)-3-hydroxybutyrate is a drink that raises blood D-beta-hydroxybutyrate quickly. It was developed at the US National Institutes of Health by Richard Veech and Todd King and later sold by companies including KetoneAid, TDeltaS and HVMN, according to Wikipedia. 
It is the best-studied exogenous ketone. Studies in healthy adults examined its kinetics and tolerability, effects on endurance fuel use in athletes, and appetite hormones. 
Its place in fat-loss discussions rests on one report of lower ghrelin and appetite; no published trial located in the sources reviewed tests it for fat loss or appearance.

name: Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate

angle.text: This ketone triglyceride (3GHB) is discussed in ketone-supplement circles as a way to raise BHB, with fat loss as the hoped-for outcome. Human work so far is limited to pharmacokinetic studies.

summary: A ketone triglyceride (3GHB) that releases beta-hydroxybutyrate; human work so far is limited to pharmacokinetic studies.
note: Not authorized as an EU novel food; an application is pending per the Commission summary cited.
currentQuick:
Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate is a water-soluble oil in which glycerol carries three beta-hydroxybutyrate groups, one of the ketone bodies. It is discussed as an exogenous ketone source, in the fat-loss and metabolism category.
The human studies registered for it are pharmacokinetic studies in healthy volunteers; no efficacy trials for fat loss or appearance appear in the sources.
How it works: After ingestion the ester groups are expected to be cleaved by lipases and esterases, releasing beta-hydroxybutyrate and glycerol into the circulation, where tissues can burn the ketone.
Risks and caveats: A 2025 toxicology package sponsored for novel-food use reported no genotoxicity and no adverse effects in a 90-day rat study. Human safety data are limited, and the compound is the subject of a pending EU novel-food application, not an authorization.
deepLead:
Glyceryl tris-3-hydroxybutyrate (3GHB, also tri-betahydroxybutyrin) is a synthetic triglyceride in which glycerol is fully esterified with beta-hydroxybutyric acid, a ketone body. It has the formula C15H26O9 and is a water-soluble clear oil. It is not itself a ketone.
Its synthesis and a seven-day infusion in rats were reported in 1997 by Birkhahn and colleagues, with support from Eastman Chemical Company, as a candidate parenteral nutrient. It is discussed alongside ketone esters and salts as an exogenous ketone, a category reviewed in the context of ketone body therapy.
Human studies registered for the compound are pharmacokinetic studies in healthy volunteers, not efficacy trials. The sources reviewed contain no study of it for fat loss or appearance.

name: R-1,3-butanediol

angle.text: R-1,3-butanediol is used in the ketone-supplement field as a precursor that raises blood ketones, with fat loss as the hoped-for outcome. Human evidence for appearance or fat loss is not established.

summary: A diol the body converts into the ketone beta-hydroxybutyrate; human evidence for appearance or fat loss is not established in the sources.
note: Do not confuse with 1,4-butanediol, which converts to GHB.
currentQuick:
R-1,3-butanediol is the (R) form of a four-carbon diol that appears in the exogenous ketone literature as a precursor of beta-hydroxybutyrate. It is also a component of some ketone esters.
Its place in the fat-loss category rests on the idea that raising ketones may affect hunger or metabolism. The sources reviewed contain no trial testing it for fat loss or appearance.
How it works: Wikipedia's ketone ester article states that R-1,3-butanediol raises blood ketones, by about 60 percent relative to the monoester according to that page. Wikipedia also notes exogenous ketones lower blood glucose and may reduce ghrelin, with insulin's role unclear.
Risks and caveats: 1,3-butanediol is recognized by the US FDA as a safe food ingredient (21 CFR 172.712) per Wikipedia. Pure chemical hazard notes include eye irritation. A study of a ketone diester in professional cyclists reported impaired time-trial performance.
deepLead:
1,3-Butanediol (C4H10O2) is a diol and secondary alcohol, a bittersweet water-soluble liquid used as a solvent, flavor-additive carrier, and intermediate for resins. The (R) enantiomer has CAS number 6290-03-5. In the exogenous ketone field, R-1,3-butanediol is described as a compound that significantly raises blood ketone levels and is a component of ketone esters developed at the NIH by Richard Veech and Todd King.
The US FDA recognizes 1,3-butanediol as a safe food ingredient under 21 CFR 172.712. The Wikipedia article describes preliminary study of it for exercise recovery and as a possible oral ketone agent in anorexia nervosa research, but states that high production cost limits adoption.
The sources reviewed contain no controlled trial of R-1,3-butanediol for fat loss or physical appearance.

name: Alanyl-glutamine

angle.text: Alanyl-glutamine is a stable glutamine dipeptide that some lifters consider for muscle recovery and retention. Its research is in hospital nutrition, such as muscle glutamine loss after surgery; no trials target physique or appearance.

summary: A stable glutamine dipeptide studied mainly in hospital nutrition, with no trials found for physique or appearance goals.
note: Research is in surgery, critical illness and gut disease; trial results are mixed.
currentQuick:
Alanyl-glutamine is a synthetic dipeptide of alanine and glutamine. It was developed so glutamine could be given in a stable, water-soluble form, and appears mainly in clinical nutrition research.
It is also discussed in the muscle category as a glutamine form, but the reference material reviewed contains no trials of it for muscle growth or appearance in healthy people.
How it works: Given intravenously, the dipeptide supplies glutamine to tissues. Trials in surgical patients examined whether this limits the fall in muscle glutamine and protein synthesis after surgery or injury.
Risks and caveats: Reported trials are in hospital patients and results vary, including a randomized study that found no benefit in autologous transplant patients. No safety data from healthy-lifter use appears in the reference material.
deepLead:
Alanyl-glutamine (L-alanyl-L-glutamine) is a synthetic dipeptide used as a glutamine source in clinical nutrition. A 1989 randomized Lancet study in 12 patients after colorectal cancer surgery gave it in parenteral nutrition and examined muscle glutamine loss and nitrogen balance.
Research since then has covered surgery, trauma, critical illness, intestinal disease, infection and malnutrition. The reference material contains no trials of alanyl-glutamine for muscle gain or appearance in healthy people.

name: Glutamine

chain: Supplies muscle's main free amino acid
angle.text: Glutamine is taken by lifters as a recovery supplement so they can train harder and build more muscle. Its clinical evidence is in medical settings such as illness and injury, not physique.

summary: The most abundant amino acid in blood, sold as a muscle-recovery supplement; its clinical evidence lies in medicine, not physique.
note: A prescription L-glutamine powder is FDA-approved for sickle cell disease; no trials in the reference material test it for muscle gain.
currentQuick:
Glutamine is a conditionally essential amino acid that the body makes in large amounts, mostly in muscle. It is sold as a supplement, often to people who lift weights, with the idea that it supports recovery and muscle retention.
The documented clinical uses are medical. A prescription form was approved by the US FDA in 2017 for sickle cell disease, and it is used in some hospital nutrition settings, where evidence is described as low quality.
How it works: Glutamine is a protein building block, a nitrogen carrier between organs, and a fuel for gut-lining and immune cells. It is also used to make glutathione. Supplement marketing builds on these roles, but the reference sources reviewed here do not report trials showing muscle growth in healthy lifters.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia describes supplemental glutamine as considered safe in adults, with an observed safe level of 14 g/day in healthy adults, and notes adverse effects in people on home parenteral nutrition or with liver abnormalities. Side effects of the prescription form include constipation, nausea, headache and abdominal pain.
deepLead:
Glutamine (Gln, Q) is an alpha-amino acid used in protein synthesis and the most abundant free amino acid in human blood. It is classed as non-essential but conditionally essential, because demand can exceed supply during stress such as illness or injury. Roughly 90 percent of it is made in muscle tissue, and the intestines, kidneys, activated immune cells and many cancer cells use it heavily.
In appearance-related communities it is sold as a supplement for muscle recovery and muscle preservation, and it appears in combination products marketed for body composition. Its documented clinical uses are different: an oral L-glutamine powder was approved by the US FDA in 2017 for reducing complications of sickle cell disease, and glutamine has been studied in surgery, critical illness and gut disorders.
Wikipedia's article does not discuss bodybuilding or athletic performance evidence, and the reference material reviewed for this entry contains no trial of glutamine supplementation for muscle gain in healthy people.
